title: Sharing Out the Priests' Duties Fairly
overview: This chapter records how the priests and their Levite helpers were sorted into family groups and given their turns of temple service by drawing lots.

parts.label: Aaron's two surviving lines (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Priests had to descend from Aaron, Israel's first high priest, but his two oldest sons died childless during his lifetime (the story is in Leviticus 10). So every priest traced his family back to one of the two younger sons, Eleazar or Ithamar.

parts.label: A fair and public draw (vv. 3-6)
parts.note: Eleazar's line had more family heads, so it received sixteen groups to Ithamar's eight, and the order of service was settled by drawing lots so no one could claim favoritism. This was done openly before the king and leaders, with a Levite scribe recording each name, though it is unclear why Ahimelek appears here where other books name his father Abiathar.

parts.label: Twenty-four shifts of priests (vv. 7-19)
parts.note: Each family group took its turn serving at the temple in this fixed order, and later Jewish sources describe each group serving about a week at a time, so each served roughly twice a year. The system lasted for centuries, and the Gospel of Luke says Zechariah, father of John the Baptist, belonged to the eighth group, Abijah's.

parts.label: The other Levite families (vv. 20-30)
parts.note: These are leaders of Levite families who were not priests but assisted them in temple work. Many names repeat the list in chapter 23, here carried down another generation.

parts.label: Oldest and youngest treated alike (v. 31)
parts.note: The Levites also drew lots for their turns, in the same public setting. Senior and junior branches of a family stood on equal footing, with no automatic advantage for the firstborn line.

think: When a group has to decide who gets the honored or important roles, what makes a method feel fair to you, and would leaving it to chance be enough?
